metadata.title: Blow up and Blur constructions in algebraic logic

nodes.name: Split and blur principle
nodes.statement: The main idea is to {\it split and blur}. Split what? You can split a clique by taking $\omega$ many disjoint copies of it, you can split a finite relation algebra, by splitting each atom into $\omega$ many, you can split a finite cylindric algebra. Generally, the splitting has to do with blowing up a finite structure into infinitely many. Then blur what? On this split one adds a subset of a set of fixed in advance blurs, usually finite, and then define an infinite atom structure, induced by the properties of the finite structure he originally started with. It is not this atom structure that is blurred but rather the original finite structure. This means that the term algebra built on this new atom structure, that is the algebra generated by the atoms, coincides with a carefully chosen partition of the set of atoms obtained after splittig and bluring up to minimal deviations, so the original finite relation algebra is blurred to the extent that is invisible on this level. The term algebra will be representable, using all such blurs as colours, But the original algebra structure re-appears in the completion of this term algebra, that is the complex algebra of the atom structure, forcing it to be non representable, due to a finite-infinite discrepancy. However, if the blurs are infinite, then, they will blur also the structure of the small algebra in the complex algebra, and the latter will be representable, inducing a complete representation of the term algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Split a finite structure into infinitely many atoms and blur it so the term algebra is representable but the complex algebra is not.

nodes.name: Blown up and blurred atom structure
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item A splitting of $N$ is a disjoint union $N\times I$, where $I$ is an infinite set. \item A blur for $N$ is any set $J$. \item An atom structure $\alpha$ is blown up and blurred if, there exists a subset $J'$ of a set $J$ of blurs, possibly empty, such that $\alpha$ has underlying set $X=N\times I \times J'$; the latter atom structure is called a blur of $N$ via $J$, and is denoted by $\alpha(N,J).$ Furthermore, every $j\in J$, induces a non-principal ultrafilter in $\wp(X)$. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ reflects $N$, if $N$ is faithfully represented in $\Cm\alpha(N,J)$ \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is weak if $\Tm\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ is very weak $\Tm\alpha(N,J)$ is not representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is strong if $\Cm\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: Defines splittings, blurs, blown up and blurred atom structures α(N,J), and when they reflect N or are weak, very weak, or strong.
nodes.definiendum: blown up and blurred atom structure

nodes.name: Family of labelled graphs $\cal F$
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be a graph. One can define a family of labelled graphs $\cal F$ such that every edge of each graph $\Gamma\in {\cal F}$, is labelled by a unique label from $\G\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $\rho\notin \G$, in a carefully chosen way. The colour of $(\rho, i)$ is defined to be $i$. The \textit{colour} of $(a, i)$ for $a \in \G$ is $i$. $\cal F$ consists of all complete labelled graphs $\Gamma$ (possibly the empty graph) such that for all distinct $ x, y, z \in \Gamma$, writing $ (a, i) = \Gamma (y, x)$, $ (b, j) = \Gamma (y, z)$, $ (c,l) = \Gamma (x, z)$, we have:\\ \begin{enumarab} \item $| \{ i, j, l \} > 1 $, or \item $ a, b, c \in \G$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of $\G$, or \item exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of $\G$, or \item two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: Complete graphs with edges labelled by $\G\cup\{\rho\}\times n$ obeying four triangle-consistency conditions.
differentia: such that for all distinct $ x, y, z \in \Gamma$, writing $ (a, i) = \Gamma (y, x)$, $ (b, j) = \Gamma (y, z)$, $ (c,l) = \Gamma (x, z)$, we have:\\ \begin{enumarab} \item $| \{ i, j, l \} > 1 $, or \item $ a, b, c \in \G$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of $\G$, or \item exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of $\G$, or \item two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$.

nodes.name: Set of permitted assignments $W$
nodes.statement: Then one takes a subset $W\subseteq {}^nM$, by roughly dropping assignments that do not satify $(\rho, l)$ for every $l<n$. Formally, $W = \{ \bar{a} \in {}^n M : M \models ( \bigwedge_{i < j < n, l < n} \neg (\rho, l)(x_i, x_j))(\bar{a}) \}.$

nodes.name: Relativized set algebra $\A$
nodes.statement: This algebr, call it $\A$, has universe $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n\}$ where $\phi^M=\{s\in W: M\models \phi[s]\}.$

nodes.name: Completion $\C$ of $\A$ is not representable
nodes.statement: Its completion is the relativized set algebra $\C$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$, which turns out not representable. (All logics are taken in the above signature). The isomorphism from $\Cm\At\A$ to $\C$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.
assumptions: Its completion is the relativized set algebra $\C$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$
conclusions: which turns out not representable.
The isomorphism from $\Cm\At\A$ to $\C$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$

nodes.name: Hodkinson's construction as split and blur
nodes.statement: Let us formulate this construction in the context of split and blur. Take the $n$ disjoint copies of $N\times \omega=\G$. Let $a\in \G\times n$. Then $a\in N\times \omega\times n$. Then for every $(a,i)$ where $a\in N\times \omega$, and $i<n$, we have an atom $R_{a,i}^{\M}\in \A$. The term algebra of $\A$ is generated by those. Hence $\N\times \omega\times n$ is the atom structure of $\A$ which can be weakly represented using the $n$ blurs, namely the set $\{\rho, i): i<n\}$. The clique $N$ appeas on the complex algebra level, forcing a finite $N$ colouring, so that the complex algebra cannot be representable.
nodes.statement_short: The atom structure of $\A$ is $N\times\omega\times n$, weakly represented with $n$ blurs; the finite clique $N$ reappears in the complex algebra.

nodes.name: Infinite $N$ gives complete representability
nodes.statement: We note that if $N$ is infinite, then the complex algebra (which is the completion of the algebra constructed as above ) will be representable and so $\A$, together the term algebra will be completely representable.

nodes.name: Relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$
nodes.statement: We define a relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$ of the form $(\{1'\}\cup (\G\times n), R_{1'}, \breve{R}, R_;)$. The only identity atom is $1'$. All atoms are self converse, so $\breve{R}=\{(a, a): a \text { an atom }\}.$ The colour of an atom $(a,i)\in \G\times n$ is $i$. The identity $1'$ has no colour. A triple $(a,b,c)$ of atoms in $\alpha(\G)$ is consistent if $R;(a,b,c)$ holds. Then the consistent triples are $(a,b,c)$ where \begin{itemize} \item one of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and the other two are equal, or \item none of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and they do not all have the same colour, or \item $a=(a', i), b=(b', i)$ and $c=(c', i)$ for some $i<n$ and $a',b',c'\in \G$, and there exists at least one graph edge of $G$ in $\{a', b', c'\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Atoms $1'$ and $\G\times n$, all self-converse; a triple is consistent unless it is monochromatic with no graph edge (or misuses $1'$).

nodes.name: $\alpha(\G)$ is a relation atom structure with an $n$-dimensional cylindric basis
nodes.statement: $\alpha(\G)$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure. It is exactly the same as that used by Hirsch and Hodkinson, except that we use $n$ colours, instead of just $3$. This allows the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis and, in fact, the atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$.
conclusions: $\alpha(\G)$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure.

the atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism with basic matrices
nodes.statement: Indeed, for each $m \in {\cal M}_n, \,\ \textrm{let} \,\ \alpha_m = \bigwedge_{i,j<n} \alpha_{ij}. $ Here $ \alpha_{ij}$ is $x_i = x_j$ if $ m_{ij} = 1$' and $R(x_i, x_j)$ otherwise, where $R = m_{ij} \in L$. Then the map $(m \mapsto \alpha^W_m)_{m \in {\cal M}_n}$ is a well - defined isomorphism of $n$-dimensional cylindric algebra atom structures.
nodes.statement_short: Map each basic matrix $m$ to the conjunction formula $\alpha_m$ and check it is an isomorphism of atom structures.

nodes.name: Complex algebra of $\alpha(\G)$ is not representable
nodes.statement: It can be shown that the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable, because its chromatic number is finite; indeed it is exactly $N$. (This will be demonstrated below.)
conclusions: the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable
indeed it is exactly $N$.

nodes.name: Is $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ outside $S\Ra\CA_{n+2}$?
nodes.statement: Is it possible, thatthe constructed relation algebrais {\it not} in $S\Ra \CA_{n+2}$ which is strictly smaller that $\RRA$.

nodes.name: Why relativized representations break the classical argument
nodes.statement: But this is not enough; the idea in the classical case, works because one member of the partition induced by the finite colouring will be monochromatic, and will satisfy $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, which is a contradiction. The last condition is not guaranteed when we have only relativized representations, because if $h$ is such a representation, it is not really a faithful one, in the sense that it can happen that there are $x_0, x_1,x_2\in X$, and $(x_0,x_1)\in h(a)$, $(x_1, x_2)\in h(b)$, $(x_0, x_2)\in h(c)$, and $a, b, c\in \Cm\G$, but $h((a;b).c)=0$ if the node $x_1$ witnessing composition, lies outside the $n$ clique determined by $x_0, x_2$, This cannot happen in case of classical representation.

nodes.name: Neat embedding theorem for relation algebras
nodes.statement: by the neat embedding theorem for relation algebras, namey, $\RRA=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S\Ra\CA_{n+k}.$
nodes.origin_citation: Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation algebras by games
conclusions: $\RRA=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S\Ra\CA_{n+k}.$

nodes.name: Clique of a relativized representation
nodes.statement: A clique $C$ of $X$ is a subset of the domain $X$, that can indeed be viewed as a complete graph, in the sense that any two points in it we have $X\models 1(x,y)$, equivalently $(x,y)\in V$, where $V$ is the unit of the relativization.
nodes.origin_citation: Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation algebras by games
differentia: that can indeed be viewed as a complete graph, in the sense that any two points in it we have $X\models 1(x,y)$, equivalently $(x,y)\in V$

nodes.name: Algebras in $S\Ra\CA_{n+k}$ have flat, square representations
nodes.statement: Assume for contradiction that $\Cm\alpha(\G)\in S\Ra \CA_{n+k}$, and $k\geq 2$. Then $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ has an $n+k-2$-flat representation $X$ \cite{HHbook2} 13.46, which is $n+k-2$ square \cite{HHbook2} 13.10.
nodes.origin_citation: Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation algebras by games, 13.46 and 13.10
conclusions: $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ has an $n+k-2$-flat representation $X$
which is $n+k-2$ square

nodes.name: Relativized representation
nodes.statement: In particular, there is a set $X$, $V\subseteq X\times X$ and $g: \Cm\alpha(\G)\to \wp(V)$ such that $h(a)$ ($a\in \Cm\alpha(\G)$) is a binary relation on $X$, and $h$ respects the relation algebra operations. Here $V=\{(x,y)\in X\times X: (x,y)\in h(1)\}$, where $1$ is the greatest element of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$. We write $1(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in h(1).$
nodes.origin_citation: Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation algebras by games

nodes.name: $n+k-2$ squareness
nodes.statement: For any $m<\omega$, let $C_m(X)=\{\bar{a}\in {}^mX: Range(a)\text { is an $m$ clique }\}$, then $n+k-2$ squareness means that that if $\bar{a}\in C_{n+k-2}(X)$, $r,s\in \Cm\G$, $i,j,k<n, k\neq i,j$, and $X\models (r;s)(a_i, a_j)$ then there is $b\in C_{n+k-2}(X)$ with $\bar{b}$ agreeing with $\bar{a}$ except possibly at $k$ such that $X\models r(b_i, b_k)$ and $X\models s(b_k, b_j)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation algebras by games, 13.10
nodes.statement_short: A representation is $n+k-2$ square if every composition witnessed on an $(n+k-2)$-clique can be realised by changing one point of the clique.

nodes.name: Equivalent form of squareness
nodes.statement: But it is not hard to show that this is equivalent to the simpler condition that for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, all $x,y\in C$ and $a,b\in \Cm\alpha(\G)$, $X\models (a;b)(x,y)$ there exists $z\in X$ such that $C\cup \{z\}$ is a clique and $X\models a(x,z)\land b(z,y)$.
assumptions: for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, all $x,y\in C$ and $a,b\in \Cm\alpha(\G)$, $X\models (a;b)(x,y)$
conclusions: there exists $z\in X$ such that $C\cup \{z\}$ is a clique and $X\models a(x,z)\land b(z,y)$

nodes.name: $\G$ has an $N$-colouring
nodes.statement: Now $\G$ has a finite colouring using $N$ colours. Indeed, the map $f:N\times \omega$ defined by $f(l,i)=l$ is a finite colouring using $N$ colours.
conclusions: $\G$ has a finite colouring using $N$ colours

nodes.name: Coloured block $(Y,k)$
nodes.statement: For $Y\subseteq N\times \omega$ and $l<n$ define $(Y, k)=\{(a,i,l): (a,i)\in Y\}$, regarded as a subset of $\Cm\G$.

nodes.name: Finite partition $J$ of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$
nodes.statement: The nodes of $N\times \omega$ can be partitioned into sets $\{C_j: j<n\}$ such that there are no edges within $C_j$. Let $J=\{1', (C_j,k): j<N, k<n\}$ Then clearly, $\sum J=1$ in $\Cm\alpha(\G)$, so that $J$ is partition of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks.
conclusions: The nodes of $N\times \omega$ can be partitioned into sets $\{C_j: j<n\}$ such that there are no edges within $C_j$
$J$ is partition of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks

nodes.name: Ramsey's theorem
nodes.statement: Ramsys's theorem aplies in this context, to allow us to infer, that there are distinct $x_i\in X$ $(i<\omega)$, $J\subseteq \omega\times \omega$ infinite and $P\in J$ such that $(x_i, x_j)\in h(P)$ for $(i, j)\in J$, $i\neq j$. Then $P\neq 1'$.
assumptions: As $J$ is finite, we have for any $x,y\in X$ there is a $P\in J$ with $(x,y)\in h(P)$.
conclusions: there are distinct $x_i\in X$ $(i<\omega)$, $J\subseteq \omega\times \omega$ infinite and $P\in J$ such that $(x_i, x_j)\in h(P)$ for $(i, j)\in J$, $i\neq j$.

nodes.name: Least $k$ forcing $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$
nodes.statement: Find a combinatorial relation between $n,k, N$ with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ that forces $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$. What is the least such $k$? This is formulated for any $P$, but maybe the condition would also force Ramseys theorem to give the right block.
nodes.statement_short: Find a relation between $n,k,N$ (with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$) forcing $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, and the least such $k$.

nodes.name: Monochromatic element
nodes.statement: A non -zero element $a$ of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ is monochromatic, if $a\leq 1'$, or $a\leq (\Gamma,s)$ for some $s<n$.

nodes.name: $(P;P)\cdot P=0$ for the Ramsey block
nodes.statement: Now $P$ is monochromatic, and the $C_j$ s are independent, it follows also from the definition of $\alpha$ that $(P;P)\cdot P=0$.
conclusions: $(P;P)\cdot P=0$

nodes.name: $\Cm\alpha(\G)\notin S\Ra\CA_{n+m}$ and non-closure under completions
nodes.statement: $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ is not in $S\Ra\CA_{n+m}$, and from this, it will follow that $\Cm\M_n\notin S\Nr_n\CA_{n+m}$, for al $m\geq k$. Showing that the latter two cases are not closed under completions.
conclusions: $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ is not in $S\Ra\CA_{n+m}$
$\Cm\M_n\notin S\Nr_n\CA_{n+m}$, for al $m\geq k$.

nodes.name: ${\sf Mat}_n\R$
nodes.statement: For a relation algebra $\R$ having an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, let ${\sf Mat}_n\R$ be the term cylindric algebra of dimension $n$ generated by the basic matrices.
nodes.genus: the term cylindric algebra of dimension $n$

nodes.name: Hodkinson's theorem on non-representable completions
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be a graph that is a disjoint union of cliques having size $n$. Then there is a strongly $n$ homogenious labelled graph $M$, every edge is labelled by an element from $\G\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $W\subseteq {}^nM$, such that the set algebra based on $W$ is an atomic $\A\in \RCA_n$, and there is an atomic $\R\in \RRA$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that $\A\cong {\sf Mat}_n\R$, and the completions of $\A$ and $\R$ are not representable, hence they are not completely representable.
nodes.statement_short: Atomic representable $\A\in\RCA_n$ and $\R\in\RRA$ with $\A\cong{\sf Mat}_n\R$ whose completions are not representable.
assumptions: Let $\G$ be a graph that is a disjoint union of cliques having size $n$.
conclusions: there is a strongly $n$ homogenious labelled graph $M$, every edge is labelled by an element from $\G\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $W\subseteq {}^nM$, such that the set algebra based on $W$ is an atomic $\A\in \RCA_n$
there is an atomic $\R\in \RRA$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that $\A\cong {\sf Mat}_n\R$
the completions of $\A$ and $\R$ are not representable, hence they are not completely representable.

nodes.name: Rectangle $H$ of split atoms
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be a finite set with $|I|\geq 6$. Let $J$ be the set of all $2$ element subsets of $I$, and let $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J, P\in W\}.$$

nodes.name: First partition $H^P$
nodes.statement: For $P\in I$, let $$H^P=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, W\in J, P\in W\}.$$

nodes.name: Blur partition $E^W$
nodes.statement: The $J$s are the blurs, for $W\in J,$ let $$E^W=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in W\}.$$

nodes.name: Evenly distributed triple $e(i,j,k)$
nodes.statement: For $i,j,k\in \omega$ $e(i,j,k)$ abbreviates that $i,j,k$ are {\it evenly distributed}, i.e. $$e(i,j,k)\text { iff } (\exists p,q,r)\{p,q,r\}=\{i,j,k\}, r-q=q-p$$ For example $3,5,7$ are evenly distributed, but $3,5,8$ are not.

nodes.name: Consistent triples of the blow up and blur atom structure
nodes.statement: Let $i,j,k\in \omega$, $P,Q,R\in I$ and $S,Z,W\in J$ such that $P\in S$, $Q\in Z$ and $R\in W$. Then the triple $(a_i^{P,S},a_j^{Q,Z}, a_k^{R,W})$ is consistent iff either \begin{enumroman} \item $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset,$ or \item $e(i,j,k)\&P\leq Q;R.$ \end{enumroman}
nodes.statement_short: $(a_i^{P,S},a_j^{Q,Z},a_k^{R,W})$ is consistent iff the blurs are disjoint or $i,j,k$ are evenly distributed and $P\leq Q;R$.

nodes.name: Atom structure $\cal F$
nodes.statement: Let $\cal F$ denote this atom structure, ${\cal F}=H\cup \{Id\}$

nodes.name: Finite relation algebra $\bold M$
nodes.statement: Now, as promised, we choose a (finite) relation algebra $\bold M$ with atoms $I\cup \{1d\}$ such that for all $P,Q\in I$, $P\neq Q$ we have $$P;P=\{Q\in I: Q\neq P\}\cup \{Id\}\text { and } P;Q=H$$

nodes.name: $\bold M$ exists and is only finitely representable
nodes.statement: Such an $\bold M$ exists It is also known that $\bold M$, if representable, can be only represented on finite sets.
conclusions: Such an $\bold M$ exists
$\bold M$, if representable, can be only represented on finite sets.

nodes.name: Blow up and blur relation algebra: non-representable complex algebra, representable term algebra
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item $\Cm{\cal F}$ is a relation algebra that is not representable. \item ${\cal R}$ the term algebra over $\cal F$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: $\Cm{\cal F}$ is a non-representable relation algebra while its term algebra $\cal R$ is representable.
assumptions: Let $\cal F$ denote this atom structure, ${\cal F}=H\cup \{Id\}$
conclusions: $\Cm{\cal F}$ is a relation algebra that is not representable.
${\cal R}$ the term algebra over $\cal F$ is representable.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on $\Cm({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\Cm F$. But $\Cm F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while $\M$ only on finite ones, hence we are done. \item The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$ \end{enumarab}

For $\phi\in L^+$, let $\phi^M=\{s\in {}^nM: M\models \phi[s]\}.$ Here we are {\it not} relativizing semantics. $$\{{\phi}^M: \phi \in L\}\mapsto \Cof(E^W)$$ $$\A\mapsto {\cal R}$$ $$\Cm\At\A\to \Cm\At{\cal R}$$

nodes.name: Atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu)$
nodes.statement: Let $l\in \omega$, $l\geq 2$, and let $\mu$ be a non-zero cardinal. Let $I$ be a finite set, $|I|\geq 3l.$ Let $$J=\{(X,n): X\subseteq I, |X|=l,n<\mu\}.$$ Let $H$ be as before, i.e. $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J\}.$$ Define $(a_i^{P,S,p}, a_j^{Q,Z,q}, a_k^{R,W,r})$ is consistent ff $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset$ or $ e(i,j,k) \text { and } |\{P,Q,R\}|\neq 1.$ Pending on $l$ and $\mu$, let us call these atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu).$ Then our first example in is just ${\cal F}(2,1).$ If $\mu\geq \omega$, then $J$ as defined above would be infinite, and $\Uf$ will be a proper subset of the ultrafilters. It is not difficult to show that if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite), then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable, and if $l<\omega$ then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable. In the former case we have infnitely many colours, so that the chromatic nmber of the graph is infinite, while in the second case the chromatic number is infinite. Informally, if the blurs get arbitarily large, then in the limit, the resulting algebra will be completely representable, and so its complex algebra will be representable. If we take, a sequence of blurs, each finite, but increasing in size we get a sequence of algebras that are not completely representable, and the sequence of their complex algebras will not be representable. The limit of the former, will be completely representable (with an infinite set of blurs); its completion will be the limit of the second sequence of non representable, will be representable. Either construction can be used to achieve this. This phenomena has many reincarnations in the literature. One is the following: It is is nothing more than Monk's classical non finite axiomatizability result; it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement: For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then $\Cm{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus $\Tm{\cal F}(i,1)$ are $\RRA$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also $\Cm{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result. We prove the cylindric case. Take $\G_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of $\A_i$, as constructed above. Then $\Cm \A_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}\Cm\A_i=\Cm(\prod_{i\in \omega}\A_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.

nodes.statement_short: Ultraproducts of the non-representable ${\cal F}(i,1)$ (resp. clique-based $\A_i$) are completely representable, so the classes are not finitely axiomatizable.

nodes.name: Part (2): representability of the term algebra
nodes.statement: The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$

By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$
nodes.statement_short: Show $rep$ is an embedding into $R(G)$.

nodes.name: Define $rep$
nodes.statement: For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding.
nodes.statement_short: Define $rep(X)$ as the edges whose label contains $X$.

nodes.name: Boolean, identity and converse
nodes.statement: $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph.
nodes.statement_short: $rep$ preserves Boolean operations, identity and converse.

nodes.name: Composition inclusion $\subseteq$
nodes.statement: From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$
nodes.statement_short: Consistency gives $rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y)$.

nodes.name: Composition inclusion $\supseteq$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$
nodes.statement_short: Completeness gives $rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to finding consistent $F,K$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to find ultrafilters $F\ni X$, $K\ni Y$ forming a consistent triple.

nodes.name: Case 1: principal label
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Principal label $U^a$: pick atoms $b\in X$, $c\in Y$.

nodes.name: Case 1 hypothesis
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$
nodes.statement_short: $l(u,v)=U^a$ gives $a\in X;Y$.

nodes.name: Case 1 witnesses
nodes.statement: Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Atoms below $X$, $Y$ give a consistent triple.

nodes.name: Case 2: non-principal label
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$
nodes.statement_short: Non-principal label $U^W$: split on finiteness of $X,Y$.

nodes.name: Case 2 hypothesis
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$.
nodes.statement_short: $X;Y$ meets $E^W$ infinitely.

nodes.name: Both finite
nodes.statement: Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i).
nodes.statement_short: Finite $X,Y$: use condition (i).

nodes.name: One infinite
nodes.statement: Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$
nodes.statement_short: Infinite $X$: use condition (ii).

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$
nodes.statement_short: $rep$ is one-to-one since every atom is realised.

nodes.name: Use the second construction
nodes.statement: For the second we use the second construction.
nodes.statement_short: Use the blow up and blur atom structures.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Ultraproduct is completely representable
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then $\Cm{\cal D}$ is completely representable.
nodes.statement_short: A non-trivial ultraproduct of ${\cal F}(i,1)$ is completely representable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Relation algebra case concluded
nodes.statement: Thus $\Tm{\cal F}(i,1)$ are $\RRA$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also $\Cm{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Non-representable algebras with representable ultraproduct give non-finite axiomatizability.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Cylindric case: clique graphs
nodes.statement: We prove the cylindric case. Take $\G_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of $\A_i$, as constructed above.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\G_i$ disjoint unions of growing cliques and their algebras $\A_i$.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Cylindric ultraproduct representable
nodes.statement: Then $\Cm \A_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}\Cm\A_i=\Cm(\prod_{i\in \omega}\A_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.
nodes.statement_short: Each $\Cm\A_i$ is non-representable but their ultraproduct is representable.
